---
title: "Reading pairs plots of posterior draws"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A histogram of $\mu$ tells us which values of $\mu$ occurred frequently. A
separate histogram of $\sigma$ does the same for $\sigma$. But those two
histograms remove the pairing between the values. They cannot tell us whether
a large value of $\mu$ tends to occur in the same posterior draw as a large or
small value of $\sigma$.

A [**pairs plot**](https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/articles/plotting-mcmc-draws.html)
retains that pairing. Each point represents one joint draw: its horizontal
coordinate is the draw's value of $\mu$, and its vertical coordinate is the
same draw's value of $\sigma$. A diagonal cloud reveals a direction along
which the parameters vary together. A curved or narrowing cloud may reveal
geometry that a constant [mass matrix](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd) cannot fully
rescale.

Pairs plots also let us attach a computational warning to the parameter values
at which it occurred. We will first read the joint geometry of the adapted
NUTS draws. We will then mark the divergent transitions from the deliberately
coarse calculation on the [preceding page](divergent-transitions.qmd). Keeping
the two displays separate prevents the diagnostic calculation from being
mistaken for posterior evidence.

## Geometry of the adapted NUTS draws

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-pair-draws
library(ggplot2)
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
adapted_draws <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(subset_draws(
  cache$production_draws, variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)))
coarse_draws <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(subset_draws(
  cache$stress_draws, variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)))
coarse_diagnostics <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(cache$stress_diagnostics))
coarse_draws$divergent <- as.logical(coarse_diagnostics$divergent__)

adapted_correlation <- cor(adapted_draws$mu, adapted_draws$sigma)
coarse_correlation <- cor(coarse_draws$mu, coarse_draws$sigma)
stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L, nrow(adapted_draws) == 4000L,
          nrow(coarse_draws) == 1000L,
          sum(coarse_draws$divergent) > 0L)
data.frame(
  transitions = c("adapted NUTS draws",
                  "deliberately coarse unadapted transitions"),
  correlation = c(adapted_correlation, coarse_correlation)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-production-pairs
#| fig-cap: "Joint mu and sigma draws from four adapted NUTS chains for the passage-level Student-t model."
adapted_opacity <- .18
ggplot(adapted_draws, aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey35", alpha = adapted_opacity, size = .65) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

A roughly circular cloud suggests weak linear dependence for this parameter pair, while a diagonal ellipse suggests that combinations along one direction remain plausible. Curvature or changing width may be more difficult for a constant mass matrix. Shape alone does not identify its cause.

The joint distribution contains information that the two marginal histograms remove: $\mu$ and $\sigma$ can each have a smooth one-dimensional histogram while their allowed combinations form a narrow ellipse or curved funnel. A sampler must move through that joint set rather than through each marginal independently.

## Locating divergences in the coarse transitions {#locating-the-stress-warning}

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-stress-pairs
#| fig-cap: "Joint locations from deliberately coarse, unadapted transitions. Accent points mark divergences; these transitions are not used for posterior summaries."
coarse_opacity <- .35
divergent_opacity <- .75
ggplot(coarse_draws, aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey68", alpha = coarse_opacity, size = .75) +
  geom_point(data = subset(coarse_draws, divergent),
             color = "#8B1A1A", alpha = divergent_opacity, size = 1.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.015, .035), ylim = c(.025, .070)) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

Marked transitions locate where the intentionally degraded integrator failed.
They do not contribute posterior evidence about $\mu$ or $\sigma$, and we do
not combine them with the adapted draws.

The accent overlay joins each coarse transition's coordinates to
`divergent__`. Clustering in one corner would identify a region where the
degraded trajectory struggled; a diffuse overlay would suggest a less
localized failure. In either case, the overlay locates a symptom and does not
by itself identify its cause.

A matrix of every parameter pair quickly becomes unreadable. Select pairs implicated by the model structure or another diagnostic. A compact cloud establishes neither causal relations among parameters nor model fit; both claims require additional assumptions or checks.

## Recap and forward link

1. Marginal adequacy does not guarantee benign joint geometry.
2. Ellipses, curvature, and changing width diagnose different joint shapes.
3. Divergence overlays locate numerical warnings; the marked diagnostic transitions remain outside the posterior summary.
4. Reproducing linguistic observations requires posterior predictive checks beyond a pairs plot.

The [generated-quantities page](generated-quantities.qmd#three-passage-level-student-t-model-outputs) turns from sampler diagnostics to derived posterior outputs.

## Check your understanding

1. What does a diagonal posterior cloud show directly?
2. What can a divergence overlay locate?
3. Why are the adapted-draw and coarse-transition displays separated?
4. Why does a compact pairs plot not establish model adequacy?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A diagonal posterior cloud shows linear posterior association: plausible parameter combinations lie along a common direction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A divergence overlay locates the part of joint parameter space where numerical integration failed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The adapted draws represent inference, while the coarse transitions come
   from deliberately degraded numerical settings and must not be pooled with
   them. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A compact pairs plot shows only selected joint parameter geometry; it does not compare replicated linguistic data with observations. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
